annotations.keyFindings: Routine screening with social work referral was followed by a larger fall in burden (3.1 against 0.8 points on a 0 to 48 scale) and fewer positive depression screens (24 against 33 percent) than usual care; no difference in care home moves.
annotations.limitations: Two clinics with different staffing; not randomised.
annotations.notes: The only study that tested screening itself.

annotations.keyFindings: Nine burden tools had reasonable measurement properties; short versions performed like long ones; no study tested the effect of screening.
Among screened high-burden caregivers, multicomponent support lowered burden more than usual care (4.2 against 1.5 points); care home moves at 24 months 21 against 27 percent with a wide interval.
annotations.limitations: Tests support for screened caregivers, not screening.

annotations.keyFindings: Screening reached 86 percent of spouses, 64 percent of adult children and 41 percent of caregivers with limited English; men more often declined referral.
Only 38 percent of referred caregivers attended support within three months; 52 percent with a named contact and same-day introduction against 24 percent with a leaflet.
annotations.notes: Screening is only as good as the referral.

annotations.keyFindings: High burden at diagnosis was associated with earlier care home admission (hazard ratio 1.46).
annotations.notes: Motivates the outcome, not the intervention.

claims.text: Routine burden screening with social work referral at a memory clinic was followed by a larger fall in caregiver burden than usual care at a comparison clinic.
claims.passage: burden scores (0 to 48) fell by a mean of 3.1 points in the screening clinic and 0.8 points in the comparison clinic
claims.interpretation: The only direct evidence on screening; not randomised.

claims.text: Among high-burden caregivers identified in specialist services, multicomponent support reduced burden more than usual care.
claims.passage: Burden scores fell by 4.2 points with support and 1.5 points with usual care at six months.
claims.interpretation: Support works for screened caregivers; the review must separate this from screening.

claims.text: Screening reached far fewer adult children and caregivers with limited English than spouses.
claims.passage: Screening was completed for 86 percent of spouses and 64 percent of adult children, who attended visits less often.
claims.interpretation: The review should extract results by relationship and language.

claims.text: Only 38 percent of caregivers referred after a high burden score attended support within three months.
claims.passage: Only 38 percent attended the support service within three months.
claims.interpretation: Referral uptake is an outcome in its own right.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Only one controlled study tested screening itself and found a modest additional fall in burden; a randomised trial shows that support helps caregivers once they are identified. Screening misses adult children and caregivers with limited English, and most referred caregivers never reach support. High burden predicts earlier care home admission, but no study shows that screening delays it. The evidence justifies a review that separates screening from support.
gradeRationale: One non-randomised study of screening, indirect randomised evidence on support, and observational equity and uptake data; serious risk of bias and indirectness.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four claims recorded; overall certainty low.
